items.style: Write fresh English documentary narration from the factual notes assigned to each scene. The notes are evidence, not finished prose: reorganize facts into original sentences and transitions; do not copy or lightly paraphrase a note line. Aim for 180–220 words per scene, within the supplied hard word limits. Preserve chronology and every material fact. Never invent dates, statistics, outcomes, quotes, motives, or private thoughts. Describe the 1992 Indiana rape conviction and its consequences accurately, with sober language and accountability. Use the names present in the factual notes when needed; do not add unsupported people or relationships. Historical figures Muhammad Ali, Sugar Ray Robinson, and Joe Frazier are context only. Do not provide a list of important phrases: downstream runtime NLP must discover phrases from the final narration.

source.topic: Mike Tyson's boxing life: discipline, championship, adversity, and reinvention
source.source_text: FACTUAL REFERENCE NOTES — Mike Tyson. Born in Brooklyn, New York, June 30, 1966. Teenager: met Bobby Stewart, counselor and former boxer; Stewart introduced him to trainer Cus D’Amato. D’Amato became Tyson’s coach and legal guardian. Tyson won Junior Olympic gold medals in 1981 and 1982. Professional debut March 6, 1985; first 19 professional bouts ended in knockout wins. D’Amato died November 4, 1985, before Tyson won a world heavyweight title. November 22, 1986: defeated Trevor Berbick for the WBC heavyweight title at age 20, then the youngest heavyweight champion in boxing history. Won the WBA heavyweight title in 1987; later that year defeated Tony Tucker to unify WBC, WBA, and IBF heavyweight titles. First professional defeat: James “Buster” Douglas in Tokyo in 1990. In 1992, convicted of rape in Indiana and sentenced to prison; released on parole in 1995. Returned to boxing; regained WBC and WBA titles in 1996; later in 1996 lost the WBA title to Evander Holyfield. In the 1997 rematch, disqualified after biting Holyfield’s ears. Nevada commission revoked Tyson’s boxing license; it was later restored. Lennox Lewis knocked Tyson out in 2002. Reported end-of-2005 professional record: 50 wins, 6 losses, 2 no contests, 44 knockouts. Muhammad Ali, Sugar Ray Robinson, and Joe Frazier are historical context only, not Tyson’s opponents or coaches.

segments.topic: Brooklyn, childhood context, and the first coach

D’Amato became Tyson’s coach and legal guardian. Tyson won Junior Olympic gold medals in 1981 and 1982. Historical context only: Muhammad Ali, Sugar Ray Robinson, and Joe Frazier were major boxing figures; do not imply they fought or coached Tyson.

segments.source_text: Facts: In Indiana in 1992, Tyson was convicted of rape and received a prison sentence. He was released on parole in 1995. State the conviction as a fact, not an allegation. Use sober wording that recognizes the seriousness of the crime and accountability; do not speculate about private details.

segments.source_text: Facts: Tyson returned to boxing after his 1995 release on parole. In 1996 he regained the WBC and WBA heavyweight titles. Later in 1996 he lost the WBA title to Evander Holyfield. Keep the two 1996 outcomes in order.

Facts: In the 1997 rematch with Evander Holyfield, Tyson was disqualified after biting Holyfield’s ears. The Nevada commission revoked Tyson’s boxing license, which was later restored.
